faq.a: Call for urgent surgical review and prepare for fasciotomy; do not wait for imaging.
faq.q: What is the first step if I suspect compartment syndrome?

faq.a: The popliteal artery lies directly behind the knee joint and can be torn by displaced fragments.
faq.q: Why does a tibial fracture risk popliteal artery injury?

faq.a: Chronic hyperglycaemia damages the common peroneal nerve, leading to loss of dorsiflexion.
faq.q: How does diabetes cause foot drop?

exam: A 25‑year‑old farmer presents with severe calf pain after a fall; the leg is tense and pain worsens on passive stretch — what is the diagnosis and immediate management? — Recognise acute compartment syndrome; urgent fasciotomy after confirming pressure >30 mm Hg or clinical signs.

A patient with sickle cell disease has a swollen, warm shin; X‑ray is unavailable — how do you differentiate cellulitis from osteomyelitis? — Look for systemic fever, progressive pain, and consider bone scan or MRI if possible; start broad‑spectrum antibiotics and arrange referral.

During a routine exam you find absent dorsalis pedis pulse but normal posterior tibial pulse — what vascular problem does this suggest? — Isolated anterior tibial artery occlusion; assess ABI and consider duplex if available.

A diabetic patient presents with foot drop after a prolonged surgery in lithotomy position — which nerve is injured and why? — Common peroneal nerve stretched at fibular head; avoid excessive leg elevation.

You suspect a deep vein thrombosis in a postpartum woman with calf swelling; Doppler is not available — what bedside test helps and what is the next step? — Perform a Homan’s sign cautiously; if positive, start anticoagulation per protocol and arrange imaging when possible.

A child with malaria develops severe leg swelling and pain; what tropical condition should be considered and how is it managed? — Consider acute bacterial cellulitis secondary to skin breach; give parenteral antibiotics and monitor for sepsis.

A patient on antiretroviral therapy presents with a painful, swollen ankle after a minor injury; what infection is common in this setting and how to treat? — Staphylococcal or streptococcal cellulitis; start empiric IV ceftriaxone if severe, adjust for local resistance.

During a trauma survey you note a fibular head fracture; what nerve injury must you check for and what exam finding confirms it? — Common peroneal nerve injury; loss of eversion and dorsiflexion (foot drop).
ai.title: Anatomy of the Lower Limb
related: Peripheral nerve injuries of the lower limb
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: A clinical overview of the leg’s bones, muscles, vessels and nerves, focusing on how anatomy guides diagnosis and management of common low‑resource conditions.

b: Divided into anterior, posterior (superficial and deep) and lateral compartments
Key landmarks: tibial tuberosity, medial malleolus, fibular head
sections.p: The leg (crus) extends from the knee joint to the ankle joint and supports weight, locomotion and venous return. Understanding its compartments helps localise pain, swelling and neurovascular injury.

b: Anterior compartment: tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus – deep peroneal nerve – anterior tibial artery
Lateral compartment: peroneus longus/brevis – superficial peroneal nerve – perforating branches of anterior tibial artery
Posterior superficial: gastrocnemius, soleus – tibial nerve – posterior tibial artery
Posterior deep: tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus – tibial nerve – posterior tibial artery
sections.p: The tibia bears most load; the fibula provides lateral stability. Muscles are grouped in four compartments, each with a primary nerve and artery.

b: Superficial veins (great saphenous) run medially, important for varicose veins and thrombosis
Deep veins accompany arteries in each compartment
sections.p: The leg lies deep to the skin and subcutaneous tissue, superficial to the tibia and fibula. The popliteal fossa posteriorly contains the tibial and common peroneal nerves, popliteal artery and vein.

b: Anterior tibial artery supplies the anterior compartment and dorsum of foot
Posterior tibial artery supplies posterior compartments and plantar foot
sections.p: Arterial inflow is via the femoral artery, which becomes the popliteal artery and then divides into anterior and posterior tibial arteries.

b: Deep peroneal nerve – dorsiflexion, toe extension
Superficial peroneal nerve – eversion, sensation over dorsum
Tibial nerve – plantarflexion, inversion, sole sensation
sections.p: The sciatic nerve splits at the popliteal fossa into tibial and common peroneal nerves, which then distribute to the leg compartments.

b: Calf pump propels blood proximally; failure predisposes to deep vein thrombosis (DVT)
Ankle stability relies on tibialis posterior and peroneal muscles
sections.p: Muscles generate dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, inversion and eversion, essential for gait, balance and venous return via the calf pump.

b: Compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion, tense swelling, loss of sensation – requires fasciotomy
Tibial fracture: check for popliteal artery injury; absent distal pulses need urgent Doppler
Peripheral neuropathy: diabetic or HIV‑related peroneal palsy presents with foot drop
sections.p: Compartment syndrome, fractures, peripheral neuropathies and vascular occlusion are common emergencies. Tropical infections (e.g., cellulitis, osteomyelitis from sickle cell) often present in the leg.

t.b: Is the pressure >30 mm Hg? – Confirms compartment syndrome; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs and urgent fasciotomy
Is ABI <0.9? – Indicates arterial insufficiency; if Doppler unavailable, assess pulses and capillary refill
Fracture line present? – Guides immobilisation; if X‑ray unavailable, treat as fracture based on clinical deformity

b: Inspect for swelling, bruising, skin changes
Palpate compartments for firmness; compare sides
Test dorsiflexion (tibialis anterior) and plantarflexion (gastrocnemius/soleus)
Evert and invert foot to assess peroneal and tibial nerves
Check distal pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial) and capillary refill
sections.p: A systematic bedside exam localises pathology to a compartment or neurovascular structure.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe leg pain with tense swelling (suspect compartment syndrome)
Rapidly spreading cellulitis with systemic signs
